blocks.text:
Design the core playback engine behind a music streaming service (the kind that powers Spotify-style playlists). Two mechanics make this problem genuinely different from a simple "play the next item in a list" queue: a smart shuffle algorithm that plays every song in a playlist exactly once before any song repeats, rather than picking randomly with replacement and risking an immediate repeat, and a free-tier skip limit that caps how many songs a free user may skip within a single listening session.

  • Actors: User (plays and skips songs), MusicPlayerService (the core orchestrator).
  • Scope: playlists, sequential and smart-shuffle playback, and a free-tier skip limit per session.

The distinguishing mechanic is smart shuffle: instead of naive random selection, which can replay the same song back to back, the shuffle strategy plays a full random permutation of the playlist before reshuffling for the next cycle, guaranteeing no repeats until every song has had its turn.
The system must support the following core capabilities:

items: Create a playlist: an ordered collection of songs.
Start a playback session: a user begins listening to a playlist in either sequential or shuffle order.
Play the next song: advance to the next song according to the session's active playback strategy.
Skip a song: advance early, subject to a per-session skip limit for free-tier users.
Shuffle without immediate repeats: a shuffled session must play every song in the playlist exactly once before any song plays again.

blocks.text: Beyond correctness, the design should hold up along five quality pillars:

metadata.alt: Five non-functional pillars: scalability, extensibility, maintainability, performance, thread safety

items: Scalability: supporting millions of playlists and concurrent playback sessions must not require touching existing playback logic.
Extensibility: a new playback mode (repeat-one, smart radio) should plug in without rewriting the service.
Maintainability: playback ordering rules, notification, and id creation are isolated in their own classes.
Performance: fetching the next song is O(1) amortized, including the occasional reshuffle, which is O(n) but happens only once per full cycle.
Thread safety: two skip requests on the same session submitted concurrently must never both slip past the skip limit check.

blocks.text: Questions worth asking the interviewer before designing:

items: Should the skip limit reset per session, per hour, or per day?
Should shuffle guarantee zero repeats within a cycle only, or also avoid the same song being first in back-to-back cycles?
Is offline downloading or adaptive audio quality in scope, or is this purely about playback ordering?
Should a repeat-one or repeat-all mode be supported alongside sequential and shuffle?
Can a user resume a session later, or is a session scoped to a single continuous listen?

blocks.text: To keep the design focused, we make these explicit assumptions:

items: The skip limit resets at the start of every new playback session, not on a rolling time window.
Shuffle avoids repeats within one cycle and additionally avoids the same song landing first in a new cycle right after it played last in the previous cycle.
Audio quality, offline downloads, and adaptive bitrate streaming are out of scope, this design covers playback ordering only.
Only sequential and shuffle modes are modeled; repeat-one and repeat-all are noted as follow-up extensions.
A playlist must contain at least one song before a playback session can start against it.

blocks.text: The design centers on four core entities:

metadata.alt: Core entities: Playlist, Song, User, and PlaybackSession

items: Song: one track, with a title, artist, and duration.
Playlist: an ordered collection of songs.
User: a listener, with a subscription tier that governs the skip limit.
PlaybackSession: one continuous listen, tracking the active strategy, skip count, and play history.

blocks.text: These entities connect through a small set of well-defined relationships:

metadata.alt: A playlist has many songs; a user starts sessions; a session plays through a playlist by delegating ordering to a playback strategy

items: Playlist to Song is one-to-many, ordered.
User to PlaybackSession is one-to-many.
PlaybackSession to Playlist is many-to-one, one playlist can back many sessions.
PlaybackSession to PlaybackStrategy is a delegation relationship: the session does not implement ordering itself.

blocks.text: Three patterns keep playback ordering, notification, and id creation decoupled from the core service.
Why needed: sequential and shuffle playback fundamentally disagree on how to pick the next song, fixed order versus a reshuffled random permutation, and that decision genuinely varies per session.

metadata.alt: PlaybackStrategy interface with SequentialPlaybackStrategy and ShufflePlaybackStrategy implementations

blocks.text: Why it is the best fit: a new playback mode (repeat-one, smart radio) is a new strategy implementation, with zero changes to the core session-management logic in MusicPlayerService. What it solves: it isolates ordering rules from the shared, stable session-tracking algorithm.
Why needed: a song starting to play, or a skip being rejected, are events a real streaming app would want to react to (now-playing widgets, play-count analytics, upsell prompts).

metadata.alt: PlaybackObserver interface notified by MusicPlayerService on every lifecycle event

blocks.text: Why it is the best fit: MusicPlayerService does not need to know who is listening. What it solves: it decouples the core playback workflow from side effects.
Why needed: playlist and session id generation should not be scattered across calling code.

metadata.alt: MusicIdFactory generating sequential PL and SESS prefixed ids

blocks.text: Why it is the best fit: every playlist and session is created through one consistent path. What it solves: centralizes id-generation rules so they cannot drift or collide.
Each class has a single, clear responsibility:

items: Song: attributes songId, title, artist, durationSeconds; responsibility: represent one track.
Playlist: attributes playlistId, name, songs; responsibility: hold an ordered set of songs.
User: attributes userId, name, tier; responsibility: identify a listener and their subscription tier.
PlaybackSession: attributes sessionId, user, playlist, strategy, skipCount, playHistory; responsibility: track one continuous listen.
MusicPlayerService: the orchestrator; responsibility: start sessions, enforce the skip limit, and delegate ordering to the active strategy.

blocks.text: Two interfaces keep the design open for extension:

metadata.alt: PlaybackStrategy and PlaybackObserver interfaces with their key methods

items: PlaybackStrategy: reset(playlist) and next(playlist): abstracts away exactly how the next song is chosen.
PlaybackObserver: onSongPlayed / onSkipRejected: abstracts away who reacts to lifecycle events.

blocks.text: Three flows below cover a successful sequential skip, a rejected skip past the free-tier limit, and a full shuffle cycle.

metadata.alt: Alice skips within her free-tier limit and advances to the next song in sequential order
Alice attempts a fourth skip after already reaching her free-tier limit of three, and is rejected
Bob's shuffled session plays through the current random order and reshuffles once the cycle is exhausted, guaranteeing every song plays once first

blocks.text: The skip-then-advance workflow, alongside its rejection branch, looks like this:

metadata.alt: A skip request checks the free tier limit first, then the strategy supplies the next song, reshuffling only when the current cycle is exhausted

items: Happy path, play: request the next song → strategy supplies it, reshuffling first if the shuffle cycle is exhausted → song returned, added to history.
Happy path, skip within limit: request a skip → free tier user is below the limit, or user is premium → skip count incremented → strategy supplies the next song exactly as a play would.
Rejection path: request a skip → free tier user is already at the limit → rejected, no song advance happens.

blocks.text: The service exposes a small, intention-revealing API:

items: startSession(user, playlist, strategy): begins a new playback session against a playlist using the chosen ordering strategy.
play(sessionId): advances to the next song without counting against the skip limit.
skip(sessionId): advances early, subject to the free-tier skip limit.

blocks.text: Three custom exceptions cover the realistic failure modes:

items: SkipLimitExceededException: a free-tier user skips beyond the per-session limit.
EmptyPlaylistException: a session is started against a playlist with no songs.
SongNotFoundException: removeSong is called with an id the playlist does not contain.

blocks.text: The critical race is two skip requests on the same session at nearly the same moment.

metadata.alt: Two threads racing to skip on the same session; synchronization ensures one skip is counted and applied before the other reads the current skip count

blocks.text: Synchronizing the check-then-increment step per session ensures two concurrent skips can never both read a skip count just below the limit and both proceed, which would otherwise let a free-tier user exceed their allotted skips.
The pattern choices make several future features low-friction to add:

items: A new playback mode (repeat-one, smart radio blending in similar songs) is a new PlaybackStrategy implementation.
A new notification channel (now-playing widget, play-count analytics) is a new PlaybackObserver implementation.
A rolling time-window skip limit, instead of a per-session limit, can be layered on by tracking skip timestamps instead of a raw count.
Collaborative playlists can be added by allowing a playlist to reference multiple contributing users, without touching playback logic at all.
Single Responsibility: Playlist tracks songs, PlaybackStrategy decides ordering, PlaybackObserver reacts to events, each for one reason to change.
Open/Closed: new playback modes or notification behavior extends via new classes, not edits to MusicPlayerService.
Liskov Substitution: any PlaybackStrategy or PlaybackObserver implementation can replace another without breaking the service.
Interface Segregation: PlaybackObserver exposes only the two lifecycle callbacks a listener actually needs.
Dependency Inversion: MusicPlayerService depends on the PlaybackStrategy and PlaybackObserver interfaces, not concrete classes.
A playlist with exactly one song under shuffle mode simply replays that one song every cycle, which is correct since there is nothing else to permute.
A premium user is never subject to the skip limit check at all, regardless of how many times they skip in a session.
Reshuffling must avoid placing the same song first in the new cycle that was played last in the previous cycle, an edge case at the cycle boundary that a naive reshuffle could otherwise miss.
play and skip both advance the same underlying strategy state; only skip additionally counts against the limit.
play / skip: O(1) amortized per call; a reshuffle is O(n) for a playlist of n songs but happens only once every n calls.
startSession: O(n) to build the initial shuffle order for a playlist of n songs.
Space: O(users + playlists + sessions) held in memory.

blocks.text: A relational schema mirrors the in-memory model directly, with foreign keys enforcing referential integrity:

metadata.alt: ER diagram: Playlist, Song, PlaylistSong, User, and PlaybackSession

items: PlaylistSong is a separate join table with an explicit position column, preserving playlist order.
PlaybackSession stores which strategy type is active and the current skip count, enough to resume enforcement without recomputation.
Add repeat-one and repeat-all as additional PlaybackStrategy implementations.
Move the skip limit to a rolling time window instead of resetting per session.
Support collaborative playlists with multiple contributing users.
In a distributed deployment, persist session state in a fast key-value store so a user can resume a session from a different device.

import random

# Strategy interface: how the next song in a playlist is chosen.
class PlaybackStrategy:
    def reset(self, playlist): raise NotImplementedError
    def next(self, playlist): raise NotImplementedError

# Plays songs in playlist order, wrapping back to the start at the end.
class SequentialPlaybackStrategy(PlaybackStrategy):
    def __init__(self):
        self.index = 0  # position of the next song to play

    def reset(self, playlist):
        self.index = 0  # start over from the first song

    def next(self, playlist):
        song = playlist.songs[self.index]  # the song at the current position
        self.index = (self.index + 1) % playlist.size()  # advance, wrapping around at the end
        return song  # hand back the chosen song

# Plays a random permutation of the whole playlist, reshuffling only once every song has played.
class ShufflePlaybackStrategy(PlaybackStrategy):
    def __init__(self, rng):
        self.order = []    # the current cycle's shuffled index order
        self.pointer = 0     # position within the current cycle
        self.rng = rng          # injected source of randomness, so behavior can be made deterministic in tests

    def reset(self, playlist):
        self.order = self._shuffled_indices(playlist.size(), -1)  # build a fresh shuffled order, no previous last song yet
        self.pointer = 0  # start at the beginning of the new cycle

    def next(self, playlist):
        if self.pointer >= len(self.order):  # current cycle is exhausted
            last_played_index = self.order[-1]  # last song of the previous cycle
            self.order = self._shuffled_indices(playlist.size(), last_played_index)  # reshuffle, avoiding a same-song repeat at the boundary
            self.pointer = 0  # restart the pointer for the new cycle
        song_index = self.order[self.pointer]  # index of the next song in this cycle
        self.pointer += 1  # advance within the cycle
        return playlist.songs[song_index]  # hand back the chosen song

    def _shuffled_indices(self, size, avoid_first):
        indices = list(range(size))  # 0..size-1
        for i in range(len(indices)-1, 0, -1):  # Fisher-Yates shuffle
            j = self.rng.randint(0, i)  # pick a random earlier or equal position
            indices[i], indices[j] = indices[j], indices[i]  # swap
        if size > 1 and indices[0] == avoid_first:  # avoid an immediate repeat at the cycle boundary
            indices[0], indices[1] = indices[1], indices[0]  # swap the first two entries
        return indices  # the new cycle's play order

# Observer interface: reacts to playback lifecycle events.
class PlaybackObserver:
    def on_song_played(self, song): raise NotImplementedError
    def on_skip_rejected(self, user_id, reason): raise NotImplementedError

# Simple observer that prints events to the console.
class ConsolePlaybackObserver(PlaybackObserver):
    def on_song_played(self, song):
        print(f"Now playing: {song.title}")

    def on_skip_rejected(self, user_id, reason):
        print(f"Skip rejected for {user_id}: {reason}")

# Custom exceptions for the realistic failure modes.
class SkipLimitExceededException(Exception): pass
class EmptyPlaylistException(Exception): pass
class SongNotFoundException(Exception): pass

# The core playback engine tying every piece together.
class MusicPlayerService:
    FREE_SKIP_LIMIT = 3  # free tier skips allowed per session

    def __init__(self):
        self.sessions = {}    # sessionId -> PlaybackSession
        self.observers = []     # listeners

    def add_observer(self, observer):
        self.observers.append(observer)  # register a listener

    def start_session(self, user, playlist, strategy, factory):
        if playlist.size() == 0:
            raise EmptyPlaylistException(f"Playlist {playlist.playlist_id} has no songs")  # must have songs
        strategy.reset(playlist)  # initialize ordering state for this playlist
        session_id = factory.next_session_id()  # build id
        session = PlaybackSession(session_id, user, playlist, strategy)  # build the session
        self.sessions[session_id] = session  # register it
        return session  # hand back the new session

    def play(self, session_id):
        session = self.sessions[session_id]  # the session to advance
        song = session.strategy.next(session.playlist)  # ask the strategy for the next song
        session.record_play(song.song_id)  # remember it was played
        for obs in self.observers:
            obs.on_song_played(song)  # notify
        return song  # hand back the chosen song

    def skip(self, session_id):
        session = self.sessions[session_id]  # the session to advance
        if session.user.tier == SubscriptionTier.FREE and session.skip_count >= MusicPlayerService.FREE_SKIP_LIMIT:  # free tier at its limit
            for obs in self.observers:
                obs.on_skip_rejected(session.user.user_id, "Skip limit reached")
            raise SkipLimitExceededException(f"Free tier skip limit reached for {session.user.user_id}")
        session.increment_skip_count()  # count this skip
        song = session.strategy.next(session.playlist)  # ask the strategy for the next song
        session.record_play(song.song_id)  # remember it was played
        for obs in self.observers:
            obs.on_song_played(song)  # notify
        return song  # hand back the chosen song

items: Why not just pick a random song every time instead of maintaining a shuffled cycle? Because pure random selection with replacement can play the same song twice in a row, or leave some songs unplayed for a very long time by chance, exactly the complaint real users had about early shuffle implementations before Spotify and others switched to cycle-based shuffling.

Why verify the shuffle demo's output as a property (no consecutive repeats, every window is a complete set) instead of asserting an exact sequence? Because the algorithm is intentionally randomized, exact output legitimately differs run to run and language to language depending on the random number generator, but the CORRECTNESS GUARANTEES the algorithm makes are exactly what should hold regardless of the specific random draw.

How would you extend this to a rolling time-window skip limit instead of a per-session limit? Store a timestamp with every skip instead of a raw counter, and count only skips within the trailing window when checking the limit.

Cycle-based shuffle vs pure random selection: cycle-based shuffle guarantees every song plays before any repeats, at the cost of slightly more bookkeeping (maintaining and periodically rebuilding the order list); pure random selection is simpler to implement but can feel repetitive or uneven to real listeners.

Per-session skip limit vs a rolling time window: a per-session limit is simple to reason about and reset, at the cost of being gameable by starting a new session; a rolling window is fairer but requires tracking timestamps instead of a single counter.

In-memory session state vs persisted session state: in-memory is fast and simple for a single server, at the cost of losing a session if that server restarts; persisting session state allows resuming across devices and server restarts at the cost of added latency per playback call.
Persist playlists, songs, and session state in a database using the schema in the Database Design section, with session state also cached in a fast key-value store for low-latency playback calls.

Emit song-played events to a message queue so downstream systems (play-count analytics, royalty calculation, recommendation models) can consume them asynchronously instead of via in-process observers.
Seed the shuffle strategy's random number generator from a secure source in production, the deterministic seed used in this demo exists purely to make the verification reproducible.
Rate-limit session creation per user to prevent a skip-limit workaround of simply starting a fresh session repeatedly.
